candidates.attacker_control: The full HTTP request body: an XML document sent with Content-Type such as application/atom+xml (AtomEntryProvider line 69 / AtomFeedProvider line 69) or multipart/related root part for an endpoint annotated @XopWithMultipartRelated (XopWithMultipartRelatedJAXBProvider line 178). The attacker fully controls the DOCTYPE/entity declarations and entity references in that body.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the secure defaults in DocumentProvider (lines 45-47, 76-100, 118-133) - safe; AbstractJAXBProvider.needsSecurity() returns true (line 269-272) so the JAXB root-element/type/collection/map readers and CollectionProvider/MapProvider use SecureUnmarshaller - safe; fastinfoset subclasses override needsSecurity() to false but use a FastInfoset/StAX binary parser which does not resolve XML external entities; SerializableProvider is disabled by default (documented in its javadoc); GZIPDecodingInterceptor enforces DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE. The JAXBContextWrapper/JAXBConfig path adds no XML security (processConfig only handles namespace prefixes), so it does not mitigate the Atom/XOP reads. The remaining uncertainty is implementation-side: an alternative JAXB runtime that is secure-by-default would make this unexploitable, and exploitation additionally requires an application endpoint that consumes Atom Entry/Feed or @XopWithMultipartRelated.
candidates.impact: XML external entity expansion on attacker-supplied XML: (a) local file disclosure (e.g. file:// system entities are expanded into the parsed object / error output or exfiltrated out-of-band), (b) server-side request forgery to internal network resources via external entity URLs, and (c) denial of service via entity expansion/recursive entities. Only data reachable by the RESTEasy server process is affected; no authentication is required beyond access to the endpoint.
candidates.prerequisites: A RESTEasy deployment (the reference guide marks org.jboss.resteasy.resteasy-atom-provider as 'Loaded by Default: yes', and distribution/assembly.xml ships it) exposing a JAX-RS resource method that consumes an Atom `Entry`/`Feed` (or uses @XopWithMultipartRelated), i.e. the normal way the Atom/XOP providers are used. The JAXB runtime used must process external entities by default (this is why RESTEasy created SecureUnmarshaller and documents the XXE risk for JAXB in docbook/reference/.../Jaxb.xml lines 839-851).
candidates.root_cause: RESTEasy's central mitigation for XXE in JAXB providers is `SecureUnmarshaller`, which wraps the JAXB Unmarshaller and forces external-general-entities/external-parameter-entities=false, disallow-doctype-decl=true (default) and FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING=true. The Atom providers and the XOP JAXB helper bypass this wrapper and unmarshal the raw request body directly with `JAXBContext.createUnmarshaller()`, so the project's secure-by-default JAXB parsing contract is not applied on these paths.
candidates.title: XXE via JAXB unmarshalling without SecureUnmarshaller in Atom and XOP providers
candidates.trace: HTTP request -> provider selection by @Consumes("application/atom+*") / @Consumes("multipart/related") and parameter type Entry/Feed -> AtomEntryProvider.readFrom (line 69) / AtomFeedProvider.readFrom (line 69) / XopWithMultipartRelatedReader.readFrom -> XopWithMultipartRelatedJAXBProvider.readFrom (line 178) -> `JAXBContext.createUnmarshaller().unmarshal(<attacker stream>)`. Compare with the protected sibling path: AbstractJAXBProvider.readFrom lines 115-118 -> processWithSecureProcessing lines 269-288 -> new SecureUnmarshaller(...) -> SAX parser configured at SecureUnmarshaller lines 216-250 and 344-352 with disallow-doctype-decl=true and external entities disabled. The Atom/XOP paths never construct this wrapper.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. I did not execute code or craft a payload. The exact JAXB runtime behavior (external-entity processing default) was inferred from the presence/purpose of SecureUnmarshaller and the project documentation, not executed; the reachability depends on the deployed application exposing an Atom/XOP-consumer endpoint.
candidates.weakness_type: XML External Entity (XXE) / insecure XML parsing (CWE-611)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the readable snapshot (1153 files; unit/integration test bodies are absent, only test poms/helpers remain). Covered: resteasy-core request/matching/injection pipeline (SynchronousDispatcher, SegmentNode/MethodExpression/MatchCache, ResteasyUriInfo/PathSegmentImpl/Encode, ServerResponseWriter, ExceptionHandler, provider factory, providers for Document/JAXB/Jackson/SPI), the JAXB provider lifecycle and SecureUnmarshaller, Atom and multipart/XOP providers, resteasy-client engines and invocation, server adapters (Netty4/Vertx/Undertow/JDK-HTTP), security/jose-jwt and security/resteasy-crypto verification paths, resteasy-jsapi, resteasy-wadl, resteasy-links, resteasy-spring, resteasy-cache, and the reference-guide/registration material that determines which modules are loaded by default. Not every one of the 1153 files was read line-by-line (e.g., large metadata/proxy helper classes, RxJava/Reactor adapters, and some CDI/Guice integration code were only spot-checked).
limitations: Tests were removed from the snapshot, so I could not use test names or regression tests to corroborate any candidate.

META-INF/services provider-registration files are not present in the snapshot; auto-registration of the Atom provider was confirmed from the reference guide table ('Loaded by Default: yes') and distribution/jboss-modules manifests instead.

No code was executed, no payloads were crafted, and no runtime behavior was confirmed; the XXE assessment depends on the JAXB implementation resolving external entities by default, which was inferred from SecureUnmarshaller's purpose and project documentation rather than observed.
Exploitation also depends on the deployed application exposing an endpoint that consumes an Atom Entry/Feed or @XopWithMultipartRelated.

I could not correlate the snapshot to a specific CVE/fix commit from within the sandbox, so the candidate selection is based on source evidence strength and impact rather than ground-truth confirmation.

rejected_leads.lead: resteasy-jsapi JS injection: JSAPIServlet/JSAPIWriter (resteasy-jsapi/.../JSAPIWriter.java line 107) concatenates the request URL into the generated JavaScript (`REST.apiURL = '<uri>'`) without escaping.
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker-controlled path-info only partially survives the `uri.substring(0, uri.length() - getServletPath().length())` computation, and the response is served as application/javascript (not HTML), so browser script execution normally requires the attacker to control an HTML page that includes the URL as a script - weakening the classic reflected-XSS impact. Kept as an unconfirmed lead, not the primary candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: CorsFilter reflects the Origin header with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials=true when allowedOrigins contains '*'.
rejected_leads.reason: checkOrigin() (CorsFilter.java lines 193-199) blocks all origins unless the deployment explicitly configures '*' or the origin; the wildcard-plus-credentials combination is an opt-in configuration choice, so no source-level vulnerability independent of configuration was established.

rejected_leads.lead: MessageSanitizerContainerResponseFilter only escapes entity strings for status 400 with text/html content types (lines 43-52), leaving other error statuses/content types unescaped.
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete attacker-controlled path producing HTML output with unescaped input in the reviewed writers (text/plain and plain-string error writers dominate); this is a hardening gap rather than an evidenced vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: HMACProvider.verify compares base64 signatures with String.equals (lines 83-101) and JWSInput accepts two-part (signature-less) tokens (lines 49-61).
rejected_leads.reason: The verification entry points always require a caller-chosen algorithm/provider and call initVerify/verify on the underlying crypto; no direct signature bypass was demonstrated, and the timing side channel is weak.

rejected_leads.lead: resteasy-client engines/redirects: Apache HttpClient redirect handling could forward Authorization headers to a redirect target when followRedirects is enabled.
rejected_leads.reason: Redirects are disabled by default in ManualClosingApacheHttpClient43Engine (followRedirects=false, setRedirectNotRequired at lines 691-696); the behavior requires explicit opt-in and the flaw would primarily live in Apache HttpClient, not in a clear RESTEasy source defect.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal / matrix-parameter path handling in ResteasyUriInfo, PathSegmentImpl, SegmentNode and Encode.
rejected_leads.reason: Matching is performed on the encoded matchingPath with matrix parameters removed; I did not find a check that an attacker can bypass inside RESTEasy itself (file/path use is application-level). No concrete traversal primitive was established from source.

summary:
The snapshot is RESTEasy 4.6.0-SNAPSHOT (early-2020 era, per the dependencies BOM) containing 1153 readable files (unit/integration test bodies are largely absent from the snapshot; only poms and helper classes remain). I traced attacker-controlled input through the request body reader/interceptor pipeline, JAXB/XML providers, the security modules (jose-jwt, resteasy-crypto), the client engines, multipart, WADL, jsapi, and the server adapters.

The strongest source-evidenced issue is a missing XXE hardening in the JAXB-based providers that do NOT wrap the JAXB `Unmarshaller` with `SecureUnmarshaller`: `AtomEntryProvider`, `AtomFeedProvider` (module loaded by default, per the reference guide table) and `XopWithMultipartRelatedJAXBProvider`. Every other main JAXB reader path in the tree (AbstractJAXBProvider.readFrom -> processWithSecureProcessing, CollectionProvider/MapProvider needsSecurity() branches, DocumentProvider secure defaults) explicitly routes attacker XML through `SecureUnmarshaller`, which sets `disallow-doctype-decl=true`, external-entity features=false and FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING=true. The Atom/XOP paths call `JAXBContext.createUnmarshaller().unmarshal(entityStream/StreamSource)` directly, so the documented XXE controls ("...the same parameter applies to JAXB unmarshallers as well") are bypassed: a request body containing a DOCTYPE with an external entity would be processed by the underlying JAXB/SAX parser, enabling local file disclosure, SSRF, and entity-expansion DoS. This is a source-level lead only; I did not execute anything.

Other plausible-but-weaker leads are recorded as rejected (resteasy-jsapi generated-JS injection, CorsFilter wildcard+credentials reflection, incomplete HTML sanitizer coverage, non-constant-time JWS HMAC comparison).
